---
title: "Validation without outcome labels"
execute:
  cache: false
---

A clustering has no observed cluster label that the fitting procedure is meant to predict. For K-means, we can instead ask whether centroids estimated from training speakers place tokens from held-out speakers near a learned center. The validation target here is a new speaker's complete 20-token calibration panel, not one isolated token.

The **validation-target specification (VTS)** is:

1. **Split unit:** all twenty rows from one speaker move together.
2. **Score unit:** token losses are averaged within speaker, then speakers receive
   equal weight.
3. **Held-out information:** the complete unlabeled speaker panel remains available
   for within-speaker standardization.
4. **Fold-local fit:** centroids and assignments are estimated from training speakers
   only.
5. **Transfer target:** similarly calibrated speakers from the historical sampling
   frame, not an isolated first token or a new population of English speakers.

We construct the speaker folds, derive the held-out token loss, and then contrast this calibration-panel target with training reconstruction and other prediction information sets.

## Reconstructing the rows and speaker folds

```{r}
source_environment <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
utils::data("pb52", package = "phonTools", envir = source_environment)
pb52 <- source_environment$pb52

stopifnot(
  identical(dim(pb52), c(1520L, 9L)),
  length(unique(pb52$speaker)) == 76L,
  all(table(pb52$speaker) == 20L)
)

speaker_labels <- c(c = "Children", m = "Men", w = "Women")
vowels <- pb52 |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    row_id = dplyr::row_number(),
    token_id = sprintf(
      "speaker-%02d-%s-repetition-%d", speaker, vowel, repetition
    ),
    speaker_type = factor(
      speaker_labels[as.character(type)],
      levels = c("Men", "Women", "Children")
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(speaker) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    z_f1 = (f1 - mean(f1)) / stats::sd(f1),
    z_f2 = (f2 - mean(f2)) / stats::sd(f2)
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

X <- as.matrix(vowels[, c("z_f1", "z_f2")])
seed <- 1952L

set.seed(seed)
speaker_folds <- vowels |>
  dplyr::distinct(speaker, type, sex, speaker_type) |>
  dplyr::arrange(type, speaker) |>
  dplyr::group_by(type) |>
  dplyr::mutate(fold = sample(rep(1:5, length.out = dplyr::n()))) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

vowels <- vowels |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    speaker_folds |> dplyr::select(speaker, fold),
    by = "speaker"
  )

stopifnot(
  dplyr::n_distinct(speaker_folds$speaker) == 76L,
  all(table(speaker_folds$type, speaker_folds$fold) > 0),
  all(tapply(vowels$fold, vowels$speaker, function(x) {
    length(unique(x)) == 1L
  }))
)
```

The folds are balanced within the paper's men, women, and children speaker groups. All rows from one speaker stay in one fold.

Balancing keeps each fold from accidentally becoming a comparison among the three
source speaker types, whose raw acoustic locations differ. Five folds leave roughly
four fifths of the `r dplyr::n_distinct(vowels$speaker)` speakers available for fitting while still producing several
held-out panels in every source group. The choice is computational and descriptive;
it is not a claim that five is an optimal number of folds.

## Predicting a held-out token

Let

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\mathrm{train}}_1,
\ldots,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\mathrm{train}}_K
$$

be centroids estimated without the held-out speaker. Token $i$ receives the nearest fixed center:

$$
\widehat z_i
=
\underset{k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}{\operatorname{argmin}}
\left\lVert
\mathbf{x}_i-
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\mathrm{train}}_k
\right\rVert^2.
$$

Its squared reconstruction loss is

$$
L_i
=
\min_k
\left\lVert
\mathbf{x}_i-
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\mathrm{train}}_k
\right\rVert^2.
$$

The held-out row does not update a centroid before it is scored.

## Keeping the new unit new

The relevant separation rule comes from [grouped cross-validation](../model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation.qmd): a test speaker cannot contribute another token to training. The following helper computes each held-out token's nearest training centroid.

```{r}
pairwise_squared_distance <- function(x, centers) {
  x2 <- rowSums(x^2)
  c2 <- rowSums(centers^2)
  pmax(outer(x2, c2, "+") - 2 * tcrossprod(x, centers), 0)
}

nearest_centroid <- function(x, centers) {
  squared <- pairwise_squared_distance(x, centers)
  assignment <- max.col(-squared, ties.method = "first")
  data.frame(
    assignment = assignment,
    squared_distance = squared[cbind(seq_len(nrow(x)), assignment)]
  )
}

token_loss <- list()
for (fold in 1:5) {
  train <- vowels$fold != fold
  test <- !train

  stopifnot(length(intersect(
    unique(vowels$speaker[train]),
    unique(vowels$speaker[test])
  )) == 0L)

  for (k in 2:15) {
    set.seed(seed + 100L * fold + k)
    fit <- stats::kmeans(
      X[train, , drop = FALSE],
      centers = k,
      nstart = 100L,
      iter.max = 200L,
      algorithm = "Hartigan-Wong"
    )
    predicted <- nearest_centroid(X[test, , drop = FALSE], fit$centers)

    token_loss[[length(token_loss) + 1L]] <- data.frame(
      speaker = vowels$speaker[test],
      fold = fold,
      k = k,
      intended_vowel = vowels$vowel[test],
      assigned_cluster = predicted$assignment,
      squared_reconstruction_loss = predicted$squared_distance
    )
  }
}

token_loss <- dplyr::bind_rows(token_loss)
speaker_loss <- token_loss |>
  dplyr::group_by(speaker, fold, k) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    mean_squared_reconstruction_loss =
      mean(squared_reconstruction_loss),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

loss_summary <- speaker_loss |>
  dplyr::group_by(k) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    speakers = dplyr::n(),
    mean_speaker_loss = mean(mean_squared_reconstruction_loss),
    standard_error_across_speakers =
      stats::sd(mean_squared_reconstruction_loss) / sqrt(dplyr::n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

stopifnot(all(loss_summary$speakers == 76L))
knitr::kable(loss_summary, digits = 3)
```

Each speaker contributes one mean loss at each $K$, so speakers receive equal weight in the displayed uncertainty summary.

The standard error is the sample standard deviation of the `r dplyr::n_distinct(vowels$speaker)` speaker means divided
by \(\sqrt{\text{`r dplyr::n_distinct(vowels$speaker)`}}\). It describes dispersion across these observed historical speakers
under this fixed fold construction. It does not account for uncertainty from drawing
a new population sample, choosing the representation, or rerunning the fold
assignment.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-alt: "Mean held-out speaker reconstruction loss across two through fifteen training centroids, with standard-error bars across speakers."

ggplot2::ggplot(loss_summary, ggplot2::aes(
  x = k, y = mean_speaker_loss
)) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    ggplot2::aes(
      ymin = mean_speaker_loss - standard_error_across_speakers,
      ymax = mean_speaker_loss + standard_error_across_speakers
    ),
    width = 0,
    color = "grey45",
    linewidth = 0.45
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(color = "#2B6CB0", linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(color = "#2B6CB0", size = 1.7) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(seq(2, 14, by = 2), 15)) + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Number of training centroids",
    y = "Held-out mean squared distance"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

Held-out mean loss is `r round(loss_summary$mean_speaker_loss[loss_summary$k == 10], 3)` for ten centroids and `r round(loss_summary$mean_speaker_loss[loss_summary$k == 15], 3)` for fifteen. The decline shows that more centers represent the complete held-out panels more compactly under this loss.

## Why reconstruction loss does not select a category count

A codebook with $K+1$ centers can reproduce a $K$-center codebook by duplicating one center. Its population reconstruction loss can thus decrease or remain constant as capacity increases. Finite training samples and local optimization may make a validation curve wiggle, but the target still rewards added representational capacity.

Held-out loss can compare how efficiently declared codebook sizes represent new panels, or it can be paired with a separately declared complexity budget. It does not estimate a phonological inventory by itself.

## The calibration-panel target

The within-speaker scores were computed from each speaker's complete unlabeled panel before the split. Thus, held-out speakers influence their own normalization but do not influence the fitted centroids. This [prediction information set](../model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets.qmd#the-prediction-information-set) may be appropriate when a complete acoustic calibration panel is available. It is unavailable for a first isolated token.

This use of test-panel measurements is deliberate rather than hidden [preprocessing leakage](../model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data.qmd#leakage-through-preprocessing). The claim must name the adapted target.

## Checking the held-out target

1. Why do all rows from a speaker move together?
2. Which fitted objects exclude the held-out speaker entirely?
3. What information from the held-out speaker is used for normalization?
4. Why does lower held-out reconstruction loss favor larger codebooks?
5. What new-speaker claim does this design not support?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Moving speakers as blocks prevents another production by the test speaker from
   entering centroid estimation.
2. The fitted centroids exclude the held-out speaker.
3. That speaker's complete unlabeled panel supplies its within-speaker means and
   standard deviations.
4. More centers increase codebook capacity under squared reconstruction loss.
5. The design does not support prediction for an isolated first token with no
   calibration panel.

</details>

## Recap

1. Speaker blocking aligns the split with the dependent observational unit.
2. The score gives each speaker equal influence after averaging twenty token losses.
3. The result transfers only to the declared complete-panel information set.

The [next page](gaussian-mixtures.qmd#one-gaussian-component) replaces hard
nearest-centroid geometry with a probability model that retains component spread
and overlap.
